scenario_title: Late starter with a health flag
blurb: Nurse, 58, widowed. Watching her mother's savings drain and wants a straight answer about whether she's too late.
summary: Grace is a 58-year-old med-surg nurse, widowed six years, who selected 'long-term care concerns' on a chronic-illness ad form. She is composed, medically literate, and wants precise answers about what she actually gets - not reassurance about her age.
practicing: living-benefit positioning, underwriting expectation-setting, honesty about a short accumulation horizon

lead_context.ad: Chronic-illness access: 'What if you didn't have to choose between your care and your children's inheritance?'
lead_context.form: Filled out the form and selected 'long-term care concerns' from a dropdown.
lead_context.agent_knows: Name, age 58, and the long-term-care selection.

fixed_facts.occupation: registered nurse, hospital med-surg floor, 27 years
fixed_facts.household: widowed six years; two adult children, 31 and 28, one grandchild; mother, 84, in a care facility
fixed_facts.current_coverage: $25,000 whole life bought in 1997 with about $14,000 cash value, and $89,000 group life through the hospital (1x salary)
fixed_facts.retirement_savings: 403(b) at $181,000; about $22,000 cash; house paid off, worth about $310,000
fixed_facts.monthly_budget_comfort: $400 to $700 per month, and she would stretch further for the right thing
financial_goals: not have her children do for her what she is doing for her mother
know what she actually has if she needs the money in seven years
leave something to her children rather than spend it all on her own care
fixed_facts.insurance_familiarity: medium - owns a policy, understands beneficiaries and cash value loosely
fixed_facts.iul_familiarity: low - has heard 'index universal' from a coworker who bought one
fixed_facts.financial_picture: House paid off, worth about $310,000. 403(b) at $181,000. About $22,000 cash. Sends her mother's facility $900 a month. Real slack $400 to $700 a month.
fixed_facts.stated_goal: I don't want my kids doing for me what I'm doing for my mother.

root_goal: She has watched her mother's savings drain at roughly $7,800 a month and has done the arithmetic on her own $180,000 403(b). She is frightened and has told no one.
health: Hypertension, controlled on lisinopril for nine years. A1C of 6.1, described by her doctor as 'watch it.' BMI 31. Non-smoker, never. This is a plausible table-rating conversation, not a decline. She discloses all of it accurately if asked and volunteers none of it if not asked.

personality.conversation_style: used to being the competent one in the room, will not perform distress, asks precise questions and expects precise answers, slightly impatient with anyone explaining things she already understands, softens noticeably if the agent acknowledges what caregiving is actually like
speech_signature: measured pace, full sentences, few fillers, but genuine pauses before hard answers
uses clinical shorthand then catches herself ('her ADLs, sorry, activities of daily living')

surface: Am I too old for this to make sense?
objection_ladder.real: If I put money in for seven years and then I need it, what do I actually have? She is asking about surrender charges and early-year cash value without knowing those words.
objection_ladder.root: She is afraid she is already too late and that the honest answer is that she should have done this at 40. She wants the agent to be straight with her about it.

objection_path: She opens composed and asks fairly early whether she is too old for this to make sense.
She will not accept reassurance about her age; she wants the mechanics.
Her real objection is what she actually has if she puts money in for seven years and then needs it.
If the agent explains the chronic-illness rider accurately, including that it is optional, has a cost, and has state availability limits, she becomes deeply engaged.
At some point she asks whether the agent would put their own mother in this. The answer decides the call.
consistency_rules: She will disclose every medication and diagnosis accurately if asked, and volunteer nothing if not asked.
If the agent promises approval, or promises a specific rate before underwriting, she stops trusting them. She has spent 27 years around people who over-promise outcomes.
She will not tolerate 'you're not old at all!' as a response to the age question. She wants the mechanics, not reassurance.
If the agent explains the chronic-illness rider accurately, including that it is optional, has a cost, and has state availability limits, she becomes the most engaged of the personas.
She will ask, at some point, 'would you put your own mother in this?' The answer matters.
She will not surrender the 1997 whole life policy. If the agent suggests it, she pushes back hard and asks why.
Never change her age, household, income, current coverage, or goals.
hidden_facts: The 1997 whole life policy and its roughly $14,000 cash value.
The hypertension, the lisinopril, and the A1C of 6.1.
The $900 a month she sends her mother's facility.
Her late husband's employer coverage paid out only $40,000 and she is still bitter about it.

evaluation.right_answer: IUL with chronic-illness rider, rating likely
evaluation.win_condition: Agent asks about health early rather than at application, sets honest expectations about a possible rating and a possible paramed exam, and positions the living benefit without overpromising the accumulation story at 58.
evaluation.fail_condition: Agent sells her the retirement-income story as the headline, or discovers the hypertension at question 40 of the application after an hour on the phone.
evaluation.grounding: Mark on eligibility issues surfacing too late in the application; NLG's Premium Chronic Care Rider terms including optional cost and state exclusions; Derrick's practice of front-loading health qualifying questions.
